readme.html:
Rail is a terminal mail client for Gmail and Microsoft 365, written in Rust. It keeps a local copy of your mail in SQLite, synced by a small background daemon, so every list, search and open is a local query and the interface never waits on the network. It is built for people who live in a terminal and want something in the spirit of mutt with threads, a unified inbox across accounts, readable HTML and a command palette. It also speaks MCP, so an AI coding agent can help you set it up without ever seeing your secrets.

The mail screen at 150 columns: the sidebar, the unified inbox and an open thread, with the keys for the pane you are in along the bottom. The accounts and the mail in these pictures are invented.

A short tour: open a thread and turn its older messages round with :thread-order, page the sidebar with Ctrl-d, turn the key hints off with :hints, and preview themes as you type in :theme (Esc puts yours back).


The thread list: date groups, an unread dot in the account's colour, the account's badge, the people, stars and attachments, the message count after the subject and the time at the edge.
A thread: the title block, the newest message open with its quoted lines folded, and the older messages as numbered cards. n and p move between messages, Tab opens or folds one.

A message after h: the From, To and Date lines above the body. The title block shows names only, so the addresses stay out of the way until you ask.
The command palette on :: every command with its key, narrowed as you type. Themes, mailboxes and the settings toggles live here too.

The sidebar: the merged mailboxes across every account, then each account with its badge, its system folders and More folders for the rest, folded and unfolded with Space.

Rail is pre-1.0. Account setup, background sync, search, reading mail, acting on threads (archive, trash, star, read, move) and writing mail (new messages, replies and forwards, with undo send, and drafts saved to the account's Drafts) work today for Gmail and Microsoft 365. Labels are Gmail's; on Microsoft 365 m moves to a folder instead.

Status

Works today

  • Setup wizard (rail setup) and a flag form for scripts (rail account add), including organisation presets and Microsoft admin consent.
  • OAuth login for Gmail / Google Workspace and Microsoft 365; tokens kept in the OS keyring, a private file, or 1Password.
  • Gmail and Microsoft 365 sync into the local store: labels or folders, message envelopes, and bodies of recent threads, kept current by a background daemon that can start at login (rail daemon install).
  • Microsoft 365 over Microsoft Graph: every mail folder, threads by conversation, read and flag (star) state, new mail within one poll interval, server search, marking read on open, archive, trash, star, read or unread and move to a folder, with undo, and writing: new messages, replies in the Outlook conversation, forwards, attachments up to 25 MiB and drafts in Outlook's Drafts. l answers Outlook uses folders, not labels: press m to move. See Microsoft 365 mail.
  • rail search over the local store and, through each account's server (Gmail's search, Microsoft Graph's $search), the mailbox itself.
  • Reading mail in the terminal: a unified inbox and per-account and per-label lists over the local store, a sidebar of merged mailboxes and each account's folders as a folding tree, a reader that opens on the newest message with the older ones as cards, folded quotes and numbered (clickable) links, filter as you type, a command palette, keys you can change in config.toml, and o to open a message's HTML in the browser. See Reading mail.
  • Archive, trash, star and mark read or unread, alone or as a selection, with undo, on Gmail and Microsoft 365. See Doing things to mail, including labelling (l, Gmail) and moving (m).
  • Writing mail: a new message, a reply, a reply to everyone or a forward, written in your own editor, reviewed in Rail and sent through the account (Gmail or Microsoft 365) with a ten second undo; drafts kept on this machine or saved to the account's Drafts, and a Drafts folder that lists both. See Writing mail.
  • rail doctor, a single health check for config, store, tokens, sync and the daemon.
  • An MCP server (rail mcp) for setting up and inspecting Rail from an AI agent.

Coming

  • Next: agent tools for drafts and sends, the last piece of mail work, governed by the per-account ai_send policy.
  • Later: search operators, layout options, inline images, display-quality HTML in the terminal.

Pre-1.0 caveats. Config keys, command output and the store's schema may change between releases. The store migrates forward on its own; there is no downgrade path. Rail is tested on Linux and macOS only.

Install

Binaries are available on the GitHub releases page with SHA-256 checksums: Linux x86_64 and ARM64 (glibc 2.36 or newer) and macOS on Apple Silicon and Intel (macOS 11 or newer). Up to v0.2.3 only Linux x86_64 was published. Extract the archive and put rail in a directory on your PATH. GitHub Actions builds each archive and attests where it came from; check one with gh attestation verify <archive> --repo vitosans/rail. Build from source on other systems.

Rail builds from source with Cargo. You need Rust 1.88 or newer and a C compiler (SQLite is bundled and compiled in). Supported platforms are Linux and macOS.

git clone https://github.com/vitosans/rail
cd rail
cargo install --locked --path crates/rail

This puts rail in ~/.cargo/bin. To upgrade, pull and run the same command; the first command of the new version replaces any older daemon still running, including one from an earlier build of the same version. When an upgrade changes the store, the new daemon migrates it the first time it starts (rebuilding the search index can take a moment on a large mailbox); until then the mail screen says the store is not set up.

Quick start

rail                       # read your mail
rail setup                 # add an account: guided steps, then a browser login
rail sync                  # fill the local store and watch progress
rail search invoice        # one line per matching thread
rail doctor                # check that everything is in order
rail daemon install        # keep syncing after you log out and back in
  1. rail opens the mail screen (see Reading mail).
  2. rail setup opens the setup wizard (running rail with no config does the same). Choose a preset your organisation gave you, or set up your own app: the wizard shows the portal steps from Account setup, opens the portal with o, asks for the values it gave you, and logs you in through the browser. It needs an interactive terminal; in scripts use rail account add with flags.
  3. rail sync wakes the background sync and shows progress (counts only, never mail) until each account is caught up. Newest mail arrives first, so recent mail is searchable within seconds, but a first sync of a large mailbox takes hours (about 250 messages a minute, under Gmail's quota). Set history_days to sync only recent mail. Ctrl-C stops watching, not the sync.
  4. rail search <query> prints date, account, sender and subject for each matching thread, newest first. Gmail's search syntax works for Gmail accounts; Microsoft 365 takes from:, subject:, to:, body: and plain words (see Microsoft 365 mail). When a server is busy or refuses the connection (not searched on Gmail or not searched on Microsoft 365 says which), it is asked once more after a short wait; the local results still print.
  5. rail doctor reports on the config, store, token backend, each account's tokens and sync, the daemon and the login unit.
  6. rail daemon install writes a systemd user unit (Linux) or a launchd agent (macOS) so the daemon starts at login. Without it, the daemon starts on demand whenever a rail command needs it and keeps running while any account is configured.

Keys

Key Action
↑ / ↓ Move within a list.
Tab / Shift-Tab Change focus between fields.
Enter Choose or continue.
Space Tick or untick the checkbox.
Esc Go back one step.
F1 Open the provider portal, or the preset's help link.
o On the Instructions step, open the provider portal in your browser.
r Retry when an error is shown.
c Copy the admin-consent URL shown with an error, or the login URL on the Login step (OSC 52; some terminals ignore it, so select the URL on screen if nothing was copied).
q Quit, except while typing in a text field.
Ctrl-C Quit from anywhere. While an account is being saved, it waits for the save to finish.

These are the wizard's default keys, the wizard.* actions in the table below; each can be changed.

The wizard exits 0 if at least one account was saved and 1 with setup cancelled; nothing was saved otherwise. Quitting while the browser login is pending cancels that login. An account whose save had already started is always finished, never left half-written; Rail then says so and exits 0. If you quit after an admin-consent error, Rail prints the admin-consent URL once the terminal is back so you can forward it to an administrator. When stdout is not a terminal, every way of opening the wizard prints a hint and exits 2.

After a browser login, Rail verifies that the signed-in mailbox matches the account's address before saving credentials or adding the account. Selecting a different mailbox fails the login and preserves existing credentials. Address comparisons ignore case. For Gmail, use the primary mailbox address (consumer Gmail dot, plus-tag and googlemail.com variants also match); Google Workspace custom aliases require the primary address. Microsoft 365 also accepts the signed-in user's principal name and SMTP aliases returned by Graph. Verification uses the existing OAuth permissions; if the profile cannot be read, finish the login again once the error is resolved.

Every key Rail reads is an action with an id and a default key. Change one in config.toml:

[keys]
"list.filter" = "/"
"reader.open_browser" = "O"
"global.palette" = ":"

A key name is a character (a, O, /), a named key (enter, esc, tab, backtab, space, up, down, left, right, pageup, pagedown, home, end, f1 to f12), either with ctrl-, alt- or shift- in front (ctrl-r, shift-tab, shift-down; shift- goes on a letter, tab, up or down), or two keys with a space between them for a sequence (g x). A key you set replaces that action's default keys. Both rail and rail setup refuse to start, naming the file and line and exiting 1, when [keys] names an action it does not know, a key it cannot read, Ctrl-C (which always quits), or a key another action of the same view already uses (a key that starts another action's sequence counts). They check before the terminal changes. A view's own key wins over a global one: q closes the reader but quits from the list. The defaults count too: J, K, shift-down and shift-up extend the selection in the list, so a [keys] entry that binds one of them to another list action ("list.down" = "J", say) stops Rail from starting with that error until you change the entry or move list.extend_down / list.extend_up to other keys. Likewise h snoozes in the list and the reader, so the reader's headers moved to H: an older "reader.headers" = "h" entry stops Rail from starting with [keys] "list.snooze" (h) and "reader.headers" (h) cannot share a key in the reader view until you remove it or bind list.snooze to another key.

The global.*, list.*, sidebar.*, reader.* and compose.* actions below take effect in the mail screen and the wizard.* ones in the setup wizard. In the mail screen ? lists the keys of the view you are in, with * after the ones set in config.toml.

Reading mail

rail with an account configured opens the mail screen. It needs an interactive terminal; in a pipe it prints a hint and exits 2. It reads the local store at once, and connects to the background daemon (starting it if needed) for sync progress. If the store is not set up yet, the list says so and points to rail sync; if the daemon cannot be reached, the header says so (daemon unreachable (Ctrl-r retries)) and Ctrl-r retries.

The thread list shows the unified inbox, newest first, in date groups: TODAY, YESTERDAY, THIS WEEK (two to six days ago) and OLDER, each name on its own row above its threads; the group of the top row stays on the first row as you scroll. PgDn and PgUp (Ctrl-d, Ctrl-u) move a page by the threads on screen: the next page starts with the thread after the last one shown, the page above ends with the thread before the first one shown, and the cursor keeps its row, or goes to the page's last thread when the page holds fewer. A group's name never sits alone on the bottom row. A row shows a dot (● in the account's colour while the thread has unread mail, a muted · once it is read, ▸ when it is selected with Space), the account's badge in All inboxes, Starred, Sent and Trash (its label's first letter on its colour), the people, ★ for starred and 📎 for attachments, the subject with the message count after it ((3), never cut), and at the right edge the time: 14:05 today and yesterday, Mon 18:20 this week, Oct 03 earlier this year, 2024-10-03 before; mail dated after today is under TODAY with its date, and a date too far off to read is under TODAY when ahead and OLDER when behind. With time = "12h" (or :time) the times read 2:05 pm and Mon 6:20 pm, and the time column is two cells wider. Unread threads are bold. With icons = "ascii" the dots are *, . and >, ★ is + and 📎 is @. 1 to 9 show one account's inbox, 0 the unified inbox again. The sidebar (shown at 100 columns and wider; b toggles it, Tab moves into it) has two sections. UNIFIED holds All inboxes, Starred, Drafts, Sent and Trash, each with every account's mail. ACCOUNTS holds each account (by its label) with its system folders under the provider's names (Inbox, Sent, Drafts, Spam and Trash on Gmail; Inbox, Sent Items, Drafts, Archive, Junk Email and Deleted Items on Microsoft 365); every other folder or label (up to 500 per account) is under More folders (N), as a tree of its /-separated path (Inbox/Infrastructure/Linode), with Gmail's categories under Categories. Enter opens the mailbox under the cursor (an account opens its inbox; on Microsoft 365 a top-level path named after a system folder, like Inbox above, opens that folder; More folders and any other path that is not a folder itself unfold instead, as does Gmail's Sent path of a label Sent/2024, which is not inside Sent). Space, ← or → folds or unfolds an account, More folders or a path; accounts start unfolded and the rest folded, for the session. Counts are unread threads (on a folded path, everything under it), drafts on Drafts, and none on Sent and Trash. Each account row has its fold arrow (▾ unfolded, ▸ folded) and a badge, its label's first letter on the account's colour. Mailboxes have icons (✉ inbox, ★ Starred, ✎ Drafts, ➤ Sent, ✕ Trash, ▣ Archive, ⊘ Spam, 📁 More folders and a path with folders under it) and their counts on the right with thousands separators. With icons = "ascii" the arrows are v and > and the icons i, *, d, >, x, a, s and /. While the sidebar does not have focus the current mailbox's row is in the accent colour; the sidebar scrolls to keep it (or, while the sidebar has focus, the cursor) in view.

The top of the screen is the header: ▍Rail │ All inboxes · 2 accounts · 22,853 unread (Starred · 2 accounts · 12 unread, Sent · 2 accounts in the merged mailboxes; an account's own Sent, Trash or Drafts shows no unread count, work · Sent), the search region (│ 🔍 / Search, | / Search with icons = "ascii"; the filter shows there once set, and the Drafts folder has none), and on the right one line for every account's sync: ● Synced 14:47 when all are caught up (the earliest account's time), else the worst state (⟳ Syncing work, ⟳ Backfill 1,200/5,000, ⟳ retrying, work stopped, ! 2 failed, ! work needs login, ! work sync failed, or the daemon's state), then the time of day at the right edge: ● Synced 14:47 │ 15:02 (3:02 pm with time = "12h"; :time changes it at once). clock = false under [general], or :clock, hides the clock. At split_threshold (140 columns by default) and wider the sidebar, the list and the reader are boxed, the focused pane in the accent colour; with icons = "ascii" the boxes are drawn with +, - and |, and an unboxed header reads |Rail | All inboxes …. At split_threshold and wider, and at least 12 rows high, the header has a box of its own too (never in the accent colour), and inside it the row reads │ Rail │ All inboxes … ● Synced 14:47 │ 15:02 │, without the ▍ bar (| Rail | … with icons = "ascii"). When the scope and the summary do not both fit, the summary and the clock stay whole and the scope is cut. While a filter is set or being typed, the search slot keeps at least 24 cells (at 60 columns and wider; less only when the summary itself leaves no room): the scope is cut first. Under 60 columns the clock and the search region go, and under 40 the summary. The status bar at the bottom names the keys of the pane you are in (Enter open j/k move Tab sidebar r reply … ? help, with the keys your config.toml sets) and shows each account's state on the right. Narrower than split_threshold it is one row; at split_threshold and wider (and at least 12 rows high) it takes three rows and each key is drawn in its own box, with no frame around the bar (+, - and | with icons = "ascii"):

┌───────┐      ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐         ┌───┐
│ Enter │ open │ j/k │ move │ Tab │ sidebar │ ? │ help        ● work ✓ · ● home ✓
└───────┘      └─────┘      └─────┘         └───┘

:hints (or hints = false under [general]) turns the hints off: the bar is one row of notices and account states at every width, and ? still lists the keys.

Enter opens a thread. At split_threshold columns (140 by default) and wider the reader opens beside the list; narrower, it covers the screen. q or Esc closes it. The reader starts with the thread's title block: the subject; the newest message's sender, its time (04:32 today, Thu 08:55 yesterday and this week, Oct 03 or 2024-10-03 before) and the account's badge and label (Dana Reyes 04:32 W WORK); its recipients by name and the thread's size (To: Vito, Tom / 4 messages, or / 4 messages when it names none); then a rule. The newest message is open under it. The older messages follow as cards between rules, oldest first (thread_order = "newest" under [general] runs them newest first): a card is the message's number in the thread in a grey box, its sender (bold while unread, ★ when starred) and its time at the right edge (▸ 2 Tom … Mon 22:11), over a line of its text. When a long thread's oldest messages are not shown, [5 older messages of this thread are not shown] stands where they would be. j/k move the cursor, n/p jump between the newest message and each card, Tab (or Enter on a card, the subject or a preview) opens or closes the message under the cursor, and Enter on [n quoted lines] shows the quoted text.
